solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Material the old man's going over as a soldier

indicators.note: the old man's own word is going, displaced from the start of the material

parts.note: paper is a material you write or print on

indicators.note: over means turned over, so the father's possessive is read backwards

parts.note: the old man is Pa, father, so his is PA'S

explanation.surface: A soldier is described by some fabric that his father is checking over.
explanation.walkthrough: The material begins with the father's name; his possessive, turned round, takes its place.
explanation.definitionFit: A sapper is a military engineer, in Britain a private soldier of the Royal Engineers.

clue.text: I also worried about Conservative Party

indicators.note: the shaken letters go about, around, the C
worried in the sense of fretted at, tugged about, so the letters of 'I also' are shaken up

explanation.surface: Someone frets about the Conservative Party too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' rearranges I ALSO into SOIAL, and 'about' puts that around C.
explanation.definitionFit: A social is a party or informal gathering, as in a church social.

clue.text: Valuable material in place moisture ruined

indicators.note: ruined means wrecked, so the letters of the two words are broken up and rebuilt

explanation.surface: Something precious has been spoilt by damp where it was kept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' rearranges all thirteen letters of PLACE MOISTURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Gold, silver and platinum are prized metals, a valuable substance traded by weight.

clue.text: Try to produce written work for tutor?

definitions.meaning: an attempt, as in 'make an ... at it'
a composition a student writes and hands in to a tutor

explanation.surface: A student attempts to write something for their tutor.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both an old term for an attempt and the usual name for a student's composition.

clue.text: One could get you having less hair maybe around front of bonce

definitions.text: One could get you having less hair maybe around front of bonce

indicators.note: the comparative word goes around the letter taken from the head

parts.note: barer means more bare, as a balding head might be

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Someone who could leave you with less hair, working around the front of your head.
explanation.walkthrough: BARER goes 'around' B, the first letter of 'bonce', British slang for the head. The whole clue also describes the hairdresser.
explanation.definitionFit: A barber cuts men's hair, so a visit could leave you balder, especially around the head.

clue.text: Coming of a king and one who would like to overthrow him?

parts.note: R is short for Rex, Latin for king

parts.words: one who would like to overthrow him
parts.note: a rival to the throne would like to topple the king

explanation.surface: A king appears, along with the pretender who wants his crown.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrival is the act of coming somewhere, a synonym used as a noun.

clue.text: Silly ego trip in bank when situation gets critical

indicators.note: silly means foolish, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A foolish act of self-importance at the bank at a tense moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' rearranges all thirteen letters of EGO TRIP IN BANK.
explanation.definitionFit: The breaking point is the moment of crisis at which a person or system can take no more.

clue.text: Live presidentially, somewhat

indicators.note: somewhat means to some extent, so only part of the long word is used

explanation.surface: To live like a president does.
explanation.definitionFit: To reside somewhere is to live there, a straight synonym.

clue.text: See about eating food brought back amidst hurrays — this fast food

indicators.note: the inner pieces sit amidst the shouts, splitting them

parts.note: cheers are shouts of hurray

indicators.note: the word See goes about, swallowing what follows

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: brought back means the word for food is read in reverse

parts.note: grub is slang for food

explanation.surface: Someone checks on eating returned food among cheering crowds at a fast-food place.
explanation.walkthrough: GRUB 'brought back' gives BURG; SEE 'about eating' it makes SEBURGE, which goes 'amidst' CHEERS: CHEE + SEBURGE + RS.
explanation.definitionFit: Burgers topped with melted cheese are a staple served at fast-food chains.

clue.text: Swimming bears in eg water off Alaska

indicators.note: swimming suggests the letters are floating about and rearranged

explanation.surface: Bears are swimming in some stretch of water near Alaska.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bering Sea lies between Alaska and Russia, north of the Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Friendly disposition of little woman hugging Italian

indicators.note: the woman's name hugs, wraps around, the abbreviation

parts.note: Amy is one of the March sisters in the novel Little Women

explanation.surface: A small woman with a warm nature embraces an Italian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little woman' points to Amy March of Little Women, not just any small woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is friendship and goodwill, a peaceable relationship between people.

clue.text: Cleric gets sanction by journalist overturned

parts.note: Rev is short for a Reverend, a cleric
to OK something is to sanction or approve it
ED is short for editor, a journalist

explanation.surface: A clergyman is given approval by a reporter, then has it reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A decision that is revoked is cancelled or overturned, a synonym.

clue.text: Unfortunate lad ending up in place where fire broke out

indicators.note: unfortunate means ill-starred, so these letters fall into disorder

explanation.surface: An unlucky boy finishes up at the scene of a blaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunate' rearranges LAD ENDING UP. The Great Fire of London of 1666 began in a bakery in this street.
explanation.definitionFit: Pudding Lane in the City of London is where the Great Fire of 1666 started.

clue.text: Money once obtainable from raid in Egypt's capital

indicators.note: the answer can be got from these letters by shifting them about
the capital of a word is its first, upper-case letter

explanation.surface: Cash once seized in a raid on a city in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obtainable from' rearranges RAID IN plus E, the 'capital' of 'Egypt's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Denarii were silver coins of ancient Rome, currency no longer in use.

clue.text: Revolutionary friends at university like a good meal

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning round, so the word for friends is read backwards

parts.note: pals are friends
up means in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: Radical student friends enjoy a fine dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'up' is the British phrase for being in residence at university, especially Oxford or Cambridge.
explanation.definitionFit: Slap-up describes a lavish, generous spread, as in a slap-up dinner.

clue.text: A boy? Quite possibly!

parts.note: a cryptic hint: someone of unspecified sex could well be a boy, though equally a girl

explanation.surface: A doubtful guess at whether someone is a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: The question invites a male name, but the answer is the neutral word for any human being, which may or may not be a boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A human individual of either sex, so a boy is one example of it.

clue.text: Moans of lots losing love including word of prayer

indicators.note: what is left of lots goes around the prayer word
losing means the zero-shaped letter is dropped from the word lots

parts.note: taken as written
love is zero in tennis, so the letter O
amen is said at the end of a prayer

explanation.surface: Many complaints, minus affection, but with a prayer thrown in.
explanation.walkthrough: Love is zero in tennis scoring, hence the O dropped.
explanation.definitionFit: Laments are cries of grief or complaint, so a noun synonym for moans.

clue.text: Generous bit to try out, not the first

indicators.note: the opening letter of the tasting piece is left off

parts.note: a sample is a small piece to taste or test

explanation.surface: A generous portion offered as a taster, though not the first one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not the first' drops S from SAMPLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Ample means plentiful or more than enough, much like a generous helping.

clue.text: A team not taken into account

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: A sports team that has been left out of the reckoning.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put to one side is set apart and ignored, left out of consideration.

clue.text: I am frailest pa, struggling as head of the tribe

indicators.note: struggling suggests the letters are thrashing about and rearranged

explanation.surface: An old father admits he is weak and battling to lead the family.
explanation.definitionFit: Latin for father of the family, used of the male head of a household or clan.

clue.text: Power demonstrated by singer — who wiggled this

definitions.text: Power demonstrated by singer — who wiggled this

parts.note: P is the abbreviation for power in physics
Elvis Presley, the rock singer

explanation.surface: A famous singer showed his strength by swinging part of his body.
explanation.walkthrough: Elvis Presley was nicknamed 'Elvis the Pelvis' for his hip-swivelling dance moves, so the whole clue points to the body part.
explanation.definitionFit: The bony basin linking spine and legs, the region Elvis notoriously gyrated on stage.

clue.text: Oxford college chaps full of silly rot

indicators.note: the men are full of, around, the jumbled word

parts.note: chaps are men

indicators.note: silly means daft, so the letters of rot are mixed up

explanation.surface: Students at an Oxford college talk a lot of nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'silly' scrambles 'rot' and 'full of' puts the result inside the chaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Merton is one of the oldest colleges of the University of Oxford, founded in 1264.
